strengths: The paper identifies a relevant and underexplored problem (efficiently learning large sets of scene representations) and gives it a clear framing ('scaled inverse graphics'), which is a useful conceptual contribution for the NeRF/3D community.

The Micro-Macro Tri-Plane decomposition is a simple but sensible mechanism for sharing information across scenes, and the two-stage training strategy (latent space + shared base planes learned first, cheap per-scene fitting second) is well motivated.

The resource-cost analysis is more thorough than typical: training time and memory are modeled asymptotically (Eqs. 10-13), the data behind Fig. 1 is provided (Table 4), and per-scene training time, memory, and rendering/decoding latency are all reported (Table 2).

A reasonably complete ablation study (Table 3) isolates the contribution of each component (latent space, micro planes, macro planes, M), and the two-stage NVS comparison in Appendix B addresses a potential confound.
Reproducibility is good: code is provided in the supplement, hyperparameters are extensively documented (Tables 7-8), and the full training algorithm is given.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: all core ingredients exist in prior work - Tri-Planes (EG3D), latent NeRF training via IG-AE (Schnepf et al., 2024), and cross-scene representation sharing (functa, hypernetwork-based initialization such as Tancik et al., 2021). The contribution is largely a combination and adaptation of these, applied to a task framing.

The headline claim of 'lowest cost while maintaining comparable NVS quality' is weaker than presented. Table 4 shows the method's PSNR (31.20) is ~9-10 dB below Instant-NGP (37.71), TensoRF (40.38), and Vanilla-NeRF (40.16). Quality parity is only achieved relative to the paper's own, comparatively weak base representation (Tri-Planes at 30.03). The trade-off frontier is not honestly discussed in the main text.

Evaluation scope is narrow: only two synthetic datasets (ShapeNet Cars, Basel Faces) at 128x128 resolution, with smooth object-centric distributions that strongly favor shared/macro representations. No real-world captured scenes, no unbounded or diverse scene sets, which limits evidence for general applicability of 'scaled' inverse graphics.

The main quantitative NVS comparison (Table 1) is computed on only 50 randomly sampled scenes, and no variance/confidence intervals are reported; differences between the method and Tri-Planes (RGB) are small and possibly within noise.

The method assumes scenes are drawn from a common distribution; behavior under distribution shift or when scaling beyond the dataset used to train the shared components is untested, and reducing N1 (the upfront 31.2-hour stage-1 cost) is left as future work.

Rendering is faster only because work is moved to a decoding step (0.36 ms render + 9.71 ms decode); end-to-end latency comparison against methods without decoder overhead (e.g., Instant-NGP) is not fully accounted for in the qualitative narrative.

Some presentation issues: duplicated Chan et al. (2022a/2022b) references are the same paper; minor typos ('bilineraly', 'nase planes', '2,23' in Table 3); Fig. 1 encodes NVS quality as circle size without a scale, making the quality-cost trade-off hard to read precisely.

strengths: Clear problem formulation: 'scaled inverse graphics' (efficiently learning large sets of NeRF-style scene representations) is a practically relevant and well-motivated task, especially as a prerequisite for 3D generative models

Well-written and clearly structured paper; the two-stage training procedure is described precisely and is fully specified in Algorithm 1, with extensive hyperparameter tables and code promised in supplementary material, supporting reproducibility
Thorough ablation study (Table 3) that isolates the contributions of the latent space, micro planes, macro planes, and the number of shared base planes
Transparent reporting of resource costs, including the fixed first-stage overhead (31.2h, 361MB) and honest acknowledgment of its limitations (e.g., benefits only materialize after N1 scenes)
Asymptotic resource analysis (Eqs. 10-13) makes the scalability claims precise and testable
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the method is essentially a combination of existing components — Tri-Planes (Chan et al.), latent NeRF training via IG-AE (Schnepf et al. 2024), and shared base representations across scenes, which closely resembles meta-learning/functa-style approaches (Tancik et al. 2021, Dupont et al. 2022) that the authors themselves cite as prior art for sharing features. The weighted sum of base planes (Eq. 3) is a simple linear combination, and the two-stage curriculum is a standard warm-start strategy

Evaluation is narrow: quality comparisons are only against the authors' own base representation (Tri-Planes RGB) on two synthetic, object-centric datasets (ShapeNet Cars, Basel Faces) at 128x128 resolution. There are no comparisons to the most natural baselines for this task — meta-learned initializations (functa), per-scene fast methods applied with amortization, or generalizable NeRFs — so the claim of 'lowest resource costs' among alternatives rests on naive independent training only (Fig. 1)

NVS quality parity with the baseline is not consistently demonstrated: SSIM is lower on ShapeNet Cars (0.9498 vs 0.9512) and LPIPS is worse (0.0367 vs 0.0346), and PSNR figures are inconsistent between Table 1 (28.56) and Table 4 (30.03) for the same method without explanation, undermining confidence in the reported numbers

All evaluations are on 50 randomly sampled scenes; the claimed advantages are asymptotic and only kick in after an expensive 31.2-hour first stage covering 500 scenes, so for moderate N the method is strictly worse than the baseline (Fig. 5)

The approach presumes a common scene distribution (cars, front-facing faces) and a dataset-specific latent space and shared planes; applicability to heterogeneous or real-world scene collections is not explored, which limits the practical significance of the 'scaled inverse graphics' framing

Rendering time comparison (98% reduction) is somewhat misleading: the method requires a 9.71ms decoding step and presumably an encoding step for ground-truth supervision that is not reported, so the end-to-end advantage is smaller than headline numbers suggest

strengths: The paper identifies and formalizes a relevant and underexplored problem: efficiently learning large sets of NeRF-style scene representations ('scaled inverse graphics'), which is a genuine bottleneck for downstream applications such as 3D generative models.

The proposed Micro-Macro Tri-Plane decomposition is a sensible and clearly motivated design, allowing scene-specific (micro) features to be compacted by leveraging dataset-level shared (macro) base planes via learned coefficients.

The two-stage training strategy is well-conceived: the expensive latent-space learning is amortized across a large number of scenes, and per-scene costs in stage 2 are substantially reduced (reported ~86% less training time and ~68% less memory per scene).

The paper includes a well-structured ablation study (Table 3) that isolates the contribution of each component (latent space, micro planes, macro planes, number of shared bases M), supporting the design choices.

The manuscript is generally well written and clearly organized, with detailed hyperparameters (Appendices C, D), an explicit training algorithm, and a promise of open-source code, which aids reproducibility.
Rendering-time savings are notable (0.36 ms latent rendering), which could be practically significant for downstream applications.
weaknesses: Inconsistencies in reported numbers undermine confidence in the evaluation: Table 1 and Table 3 report 28.64 dB for 'Ours' on ShapeNet Cars, whereas Appendix Table 4 reports 31.20 dB for 'Ours'; Fig. 4's caption references 'ShapeNet Cats' although the experiments use ShapeNet Cars; Eq. (6) uses Eψ instead of Eϕ. These errors need correction.

The evaluation scope is narrow: only two synthetic, object-centric datasets (ShapeNet Cars, Basel Faces) at low resolution (128x128), with no real-world captures, no unbounded scenes, and quality metrics averaged over only 50 sampled scenes. Generalization of the approach beyond tightly clustered object distributions is unclear.

The primary quantitative comparison is essentially against the authors' own base representation (Tri-Planes RGB). The broader comparison in Fig. 1/Table 4 compares methods trained independently, and NVS quality differences across methods are substantial (e.g., vanilla NeRF achieves 40.16 dB vs. 31.20 dB for 'Ours'), making the 'lowest resource cost' claim partly a consequence of operating at a lower quality level.

The novelty is moderate: the method is a combination of existing components — IG-AE latent NeRF training (Schnepf et al., 2024), Tri-Planes (Chan et al., 2022), and shared/base representations across scenes (Dupont et al., 2022; Tancik et al., 2021). The Micro-Macro decomposition is an incremental contribution over this prior art.

The claimed asymptotic savings depend on amortizing a large fixed cost (t1 = 31.2 hours, m1 = 361 MB for the first 500 scenes). For moderate N, the advantage over the baseline shrinks considerably, and this breakeven analysis is not discussed in depth.

Some reported values appear questionable: 'Ours-Macro' memory of 0.0008 MB per scene seems implausibly small given the coefficient vectors and plane resolution; Table 3 lists '2,23' min (typo). The amortized-memory accounting could be presented more rigorously to avoid appearing favorable.

Sensitivity to key hyper-parameters (M, F_mac/F_mic split, N_1) is not explored; M=50 seems high for a 2000-scene dataset, and the interplay between number of shared bases and dataset size is not analyzed.

The approach assumes all scenes come from a common distribution with aligned/known poses; behavior on heterogeneous or out-of-distribution new scenes is not tested, which limits the practical significance of the 'scaled' claim.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: the paper formalizes 'multi-scene inverse graphics' (MSIG) and identifies a genuine gap — Tri-Planes are popular for image-model interoperability but are resource-heavy when learning many scenes.

Technically sensible design: the micro/macro plane decomposition (Eq. 1-2), training in a 3D-aware latent space, and the two-subset training strategy (train shared components on a small subset, then cheaply learn the rest) are well explained, with a full algorithm and hyperparameters provided.

Strong empirical support for the central claims: Table 1 and Figures 1/4 show substantial reductions in per-scene training time (~7-8 min vs 64 min for Tri-Planes) and memory (0.48 MB vs 1.5 MB), with comparable or better NVS quality; the ULW variant achieves the lowest memory among all baselines.

Comprehensive evaluation: multiple datasets (4 ShapeNet categories + Basel Faces), both single-scene and many-scene baselines, an adapted CodeNeRF (MSIG) baseline with a justified choice of N1 (Table 7), scaling analysis of total time/memory (Eqs. 10-12, Fig. 4-5), per-scene breakdowns, qualitative comparisons including SPARF failure cases, and a thorough ablation (Table 2) that isolates the contribution of each component.
Code is publicly released as open-source, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Evaluation is restricted to synthetic data (ShapeNet, rendered Basel Faces) at low resolution (128×128); no real-world captured scenes are tested, which limits evidence of generality and practical relevance.

NVS metrics are computed on only 16 scenes (4 per ShapeNet category) and 4 faces; although sampling is explained, this is a small evaluation set and per-scene tables show notable variance (e.g., Fused-Planes sometimes loses to Tri-Planes on individual scenes), so aggregate claims would benefit from larger sampling or confidence intervals.

Novelty is somewhat incremental: the method is essentially a combination of known ideas — shared/low-rank planar components, latent-space NeRF training (from the authors' own cited 'Anonymous, 2025' pipeline), and meta-learning-style subset training — packaged for the MSIG setting; the individual components are not new.

The advantage over non-planar methods is not uniform: SPARF-128 achieves better PSNR, lower memory (0.74 MB), and comparable time; the justification for prioritizing planar structure (2D CNN interoperability) is argued but never demonstrated experimentally (e.g., no downstream 2D-image-model or generation experiment showing the benefit of planarity).

Total memory footprint m_tot includes a large shared component (m0 ≈ 360 MB for the latent space/decoder), so for small numbers of scenes the memory advantage largely disappears; the fixed-cost trade-off deserves more discussion.

Latent-space rendering introduces a VAE dependency (initialized from Stable Diffusion), adding pipeline complexity and potential quality bottlenecks; ablation shows quality degradations in the latent variants that are not deeply analyzed.

strengths: The paper addresses a clearly motivated problem (resource costs of learning large sets of scenes) and the MSIG framing is well articulated with a useful taxonomy of related approaches (Table 3).

The evaluation is relatively thorough for this sub-area: multiple baselines across single-scene and many-scene categories, an ablation study justifying each component (Table 2), scaling analysis of time/memory versus number of scenes (Figure 4), and per-scene breakdowns in the appendix.

Fused-Planes demonstrates genuine resource savings over Tri-Planes (roughly 7x faster training and 3x lower per-scene memory) with comparable or slightly better NVS quality, and the code/hyperparameters are released for reproducibility.

The two-variant design (Fused-Planes and the ULW variant) offers a sensible quality-memory trade-off, and the resource-cost accounting (Equations 10-12) is transparent about shared vs per-scene costs.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The contribution is essentially a combination of existing ideas: Tri-Planes as backbone, training in a learned latent space, and a shared-basis decomposition where each scene's representation is a weighted sum of M base planes (Equation 2). Weighted combinations of shared bases are a standard compression/sharing mechanism, and the authors' novelty claim of being 'first to utilize shared representations with planar structures' is a thin distinction from prior multi-scene sharing work they themselves cite (CodeNeRF, Schwarz et al., Niemeyer & Geiger).

Heavy dependence on an unpublished, anonymized concurrent work ('Anonymous, 2025') for two central ingredients: the 3D-aware latent space regularization and the entire Latent NeRF training pipeline used for subset 2. Building the core method on non-verifiable, non-archival work undermines both reproducibility and the ability to assess which contributions are actually new.

Evaluation is confined to synthetic, low-resolution (128x128) data (ShapeNet and rendered Basel Faces from a synthetic upper-hemisphere camera distribution). No real-world captures, no higher resolutions, and no unbounded/outdoor scenes; the practical significance of the claimed resource savings in realistic MSIG settings is therefore untested.

The NVS evaluation samples only 4 scenes per ShapeNet category (16 total) and 4 faces, which is a very small evaluation sample; per-scene tables reveal high variance (e.g., Speakers and Furniture categories where Fused-Planes underperforms Tri-Planes on several scenes), and the aggregate metrics may mask dataset-dependent weaknesses.

The headline efficiency comparison is somewhat favorable by construction: the per-scene time metric treats subset 1 and subset 2 scenes identically in Figure 1 despite tau_1 = 14.96 min vs tau = 8.96 min, the shared components require a non-trivial m_0 of ~360 MB that dominates total memory for small N (as Figure 5 shows), and the CodeNeRF (MSIG) baseline is the authors' own adaptation rather than an established method, making the 'best resource-quality trade-off' claims harder to independently verify.

Rendering quality still trails strong non-planar single-scene methods (TensorRF, Instant-NGP, 3DGS) by a noticeable margin on several datasets, so the method's value hinges entirely on the planar-structure argument (compatibility with image backbones), which is asserted but never demonstrated with a downstream application (e.g., no generation or editing experiments despite motivating Tri-Planes by 2D-backbone interoperability).

The two-subset pipeline introduces considerable complexity and hyperparameter sensitivity (choice of N_1, M, F_mic/F_mac, warm-up schedules, loss weights), and the ablation shows the latent space costs 63 min/scene on its own (Fused-Plans RGB ablation), suggesting the efficiency gains come substantially from the borrowed anonymous-2025 latent pipeline rather than the Fused-Planes decomposition itself.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation: the paper identifies a genuine resource-efficiency gap for planar representations (Tri-Planes) when learning large sets of scenes, and the 'multi-scene inverse graphics' framing is well articulated with a useful taxonomy of related approaches (Table 3).

The core technical idea is sensible and effective: splitting planar representations into scene-specific 'micro' planes and dataset-level 'macro' planes (learned as a weighted combination of shared base planes) plus training in a 3D-aware latent space yields large savings — roughly 7x lower per-scene training time (8.96 vs 64.32 min) and 3x lower memory than Tri-Planes, while slightly improving rendering quality.

Comprehensive and transparent evaluation: comparisons against a broad set of single-scene and many-scene baselines under consistent conditions, per-dataset and per-scene breakdowns (Tables 8-12), a scaling analysis of total time/memory vs. number of scenes (Figures 4-5), and an ablation study (Table 2) that cleanly justifies each component (latent space, micro, macro, and M>1).

Honest resource-cost accounting: the paper explicitly separates fixed shared costs (m0) from per-scene costs (mu) and discusses the crossover regime rather than hiding it, and reports the ULW variant's quality/memory trade-off.

Good reproducibility: code promised as open-source, detailed training algorithm (Appendix E), and complete hyperparameter tables (Tables 13-14). Even a new adapted baseline (CodeNeRF-MSIG) is introduced fairly, with sensitivity analysis over N1 (Table 7).
weaknesses: Limited evaluation scope: experiments are confined to synthetic data (ShapeNet categories and Basel Faces) rendered at only 128x128 resolution. There is no evidence on real-world captures or higher resolutions, which weakens claims of practical significance for MSIG and leaves generalization of the shared 'macro' structure untested.

Rendering-quality gains over the direct Tri-Planes baseline are modest and inconsistent: overall PSNR improves (30.47 vs 28.15), but per-scene results (Tables 8-12) show Fused-Planes loses to Tri-Planes on several scenes (e.g., Face 1, Car 3, Sofa 1), and both remain clearly below strong single-scene methods and SPARF-128. The main contribution is efficiency rather than quality, which narrows the impact.

The dependence on a cited anonymous work ('Anonymous, 2025') for both the 3D-aware latent space and the Latent NeRF Training Pipeline is problematic for assessing novelty and self-containedness: a central component of the method appears to originate from another (possibly under-review) paper, and the paper's own novelty reduces to the micro/macro decomposition plus a two-subset training schedule — a relatively incremental contribution.

The memory advantage requires large N to materialize: the shared components cost ~360MB (m0), so for realistic set sizes the total memory can exceed Tri-Planes (visible in Figure 5, crossover only at fairly large N). The practical benefit claim should be tempered by this regime dependence.

Some aspects of the framework feel self-referential: 'MSIG' as a named framework, and the CodeNeRF (MSIG) baseline designed by the authors, make it harder to compare against independently established problem settings; no comparison is given against learned-initialization/meta-learning approaches (e.g., Tancik et al. 2021) even in the many-view regime.

Ablations are performed only on ShapeNet Cars (50 scenes), so design-choice conclusions may not transfer across datasets; statistical variance across the random 16-scene evaluation sampling is not reported.
